lesson.title: Keep pupils’ data private
lesson.subtitle: What never goes in, and how to use AI without it

video.title: Keep pupils’ data private
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Amina Bello — primary teacher, Nigeria (main character)
Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

chapters.label: Personal data, and how to leave it out
Never in, and what to check

scenes.visual: Late evening, report-card season. Amina’s thumb hovers over the send button: the chat box holds a pasted mark sheet with names, marks and a health note. She stops and pulls her thumb back.
scenes.animation: The pasted sheet slides into the chat box; the thumb hovers; a slow push-in on Amina’s worried face.
scenes.narration: I nearly pasted my whole mark sheet into a chatbot! Names, marks, even a note that Musa missed a month with sickle cell. Then I stopped. Where does all that go when I press send?

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the course name, the lesson title and a yellow ‘AI’ track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark scales 0→100% with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: keeping pupils’ data private, and still using AI.

scenes.visual: A flow: the message leaves the phone, travels to the company’s computers, lands in storage, and a faint arrow leads on to ‘training’.
scenes.animation: A small envelope travels along the arrows; each stop lights up as it is said.
scenes.narration: When you press send, your words go to the company’s computers. There they’re processed, and usually stored for a while. Depending on the tool and settings, staff may review some chats, and chats may train later models.

scenes.visual: A chain of cards: a chat typed in, the training box, the model repeating a line word for word, and that line popping up in a stranger’s answer.
scenes.animation: Cards appear left to right with arrows; the repeated line flashes red in the last card.
scenes.on_screen_text: What goes in can come out
scenes.narration: And what goes into training can come out. Models sometimes repeat pieces of their training text word for word. Researchers have pulled real names, phone numbers and emails out of models this way. It’s rare, but a pupil’s details typed today could turn up in someone else’s answer.

scenes.visual: Clean white card with the AI track chip: ‘Personal data’ and a list of what points to a person: a name, a face, a voice, an ID number, and a description that can only mean one child.
scenes.animation: Rows appear as they are said; the last row gets a magnifying glass.
scenes.narration: Personal data is anything that points to a person, alone or with other details: a name, a face, a voice, an ID number. Even “the only girl in Primary Five with a hearing aid” points to one child.

scenes.visual: Amina on the phone to a teacher friend at another school, describing a pupil’s problem without any name. A speech bubble shows ‘One of my pupils…’; a locked folder stays on her desk.
scenes.animation: The speech bubble pops; a padlock clicks shut on the folder.
scenes.on_screen_text: Ask as you’d ask a colleague
scenes.narration: It’s like asking a teacher at another school for advice. You’d say, “One of my pupils keeps missing class.” Not her name and her family’s story. The advice is just as good.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma pops in with a pile of report cards, eyebrow raised. Three answer cards drop in below her.
scenes.animation: Character slides in from the side; answer cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Amina needs comments for sixty-two report cards. What’s the safest way to use AI?

scenes.visual: The card ‘Swap names for Pupil A, B, C’ gets a check badge. The mark sheet’s names turn into Pupil A, B, C; the key (who is who) is written on a paper that stays in Amina’s bag.
scenes.animation: Names flip one by one into letters; the paper key folds into the bag.
scenes.on_screen_text: Names become Pupil A, B, C
scenes.narration: Swap names for Pupil A, B, C. Take out anything else that points to one child, and keep the key, who is who, on your own paper. Don’t count on deleting a chat later: copies may be kept for a while.

scenes.visual: A red list on a white card: names with marks, health and special needs, family matters, photos and voice recordings, ID and phone numbers. A padlock sits beside it.
scenes.animation: Each row slides in with a red tile as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: Never into a public AI tool
scenes.narration: Some things never go into a public AI tool, even to save time. Names with marks, health and special needs, family matters, photos and voice recordings, and ID or phone numbers.

scenes.visual: Three checks before using a tool: a settings screen with a ‘use my chats for training’ switch turned off, an age sign (13+), and the school’s rules pinned in the staff room.
scenes.animation: The switch flips off; the age sign pops; the rules sheet unrolls.
scenes.on_screen_text: Before you use a tool, check
scenes.narration: Before using any AI tool, check three things. Its settings: many let you switch off training on your chats. Its age rules: often thirteen and over, with a parent’s permission under eighteen. And your school’s rules: which tools, and for what.

scenes.visual: A phone screen with the lab: the training text box with school sentences and one added line, ‘Halima has asthma’; the first-word choices with their percentages; then the sentence the model writes: the private line, word for word.
scenes.animation: The new line types into the training text; ‘Train the model’ is tapped; the choices list shows ‘Halima’; the written sentence types out.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: a tiny language model
scenes.narration: In the app, train a tiny language model on school sentences. Add a made-up private one, like “Halima has asthma”, and train again. Then let it write, again and again. If it picks the name, it writes your sentence back, word for word.

scenes.visual: Amina holds up her phone showing a chat. Three answer cards appear beside her.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Why could a pupil’s details, typed into a chatbot, turn up again later?

scenes.visual: The first card gets the check badge, then the screen resolves into four summary lines and an orange takeaway bar.
scenes.animation: Lines tick in 250 ms apart; the takeaway bar slides up.
scenes.on_screen_text: In and out · Swap names · Check
scenes.narration: Chats can train later models, and models can repeat what they learned. Remember: some data never goes in. Swap names for Pupil A, B, C. And check the settings, age rules and school rules.

scenes.visual: Amina’s classroom: groups sort paper cards into three piles under green, amber and red circles drawn on the board.
scenes.animation: Cards fly into the three piles; one card hovers between amber and red while a group argues.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: play “Traffic light”. Groups sort cards: a lesson topic, a test score with a name, a class photo, a pupil’s poem. Green: fine to share with AI. Amber: only without names. Red: never. Then discuss the hard cards.

checkpoints.prompt: Amina needs report card comments. What’s the safest way to use AI?

options.text: Paste names, then delete the chat
Paste marks; the chat is private
Swap names for Pupil A, B, C

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the AI needs the marks and the pattern, not who the child is. Keep the key to the names on your own paper.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — deleting a chat may not remove every copy, and chats are less private than they feel. Swap names for Pupil A, B, C.

checkpoints.prompt: Why could a pupil’s details, typed into a chatbot, turn up again later?

options.text: Chats can train models that repeat things
Other users can open your chats

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — chats can become training data, and models sometimes repeat what they learned, word for word.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — chats aren’t posted online or open to other users unless you share them. But they can train later models, which can repeat what they learned.
